records.final_text:
I built and delivered the rugged military supply crate for Godot 4 into `output/`.

### Delivered Files
- **Main glTF 2.0 binary**: `output/military_supply_crate.glb`
- **LODs & colliders**: `output/military_supply_crate_LOD1.glb`, `output/military_supply_crate_LOD2.glb`, `output/military_supply_crate_colliders.glb` (8 hulls)
- **Textures & manifest**: 3 texture files in `output/textures/` and `output/manifest.json`
- **Session export package**: `/home/agent/project/agy3d_assets/military_supply_crate-4c4d32/export/military_supply_crate`
- **Lookdev render**: `/home/agent/project/agy3d_assets/military_supply_crate-4c4d32/artifacts/lookdev_eevee_ad2cabe063e442199f7d4504a3e2af11.png`

### What Was Built
- **Geometry (65 nodes, 2,480 / 1,646 / 498 triangles across LOD0/LOD1/LOD2, `uv stretch 0.000`)**:
  - **Main body & lid**: Beveled crate tub (`main_body`) with recessed side/front/back panels, bottom skids (`skid`, `skid__mx`) resting on `Z = 0`, sealing gasket (`lid_gasket`), beveled lid (`lid_main`) with recessed top deck and 3 reinforcing ribs (`lid_rib*`), vertical panel stiffeners (`rib_front*`, `rib_back*`), and a bolted front ID plate (`id_plate` with 4 hex bolts).
  - **Corner guards**: 4 bottom extruded L-brackets (`corner_bot_*`), 4 top extruded L-brackets (`corner_top_*`), and 4 top corner cap plates (`corner_cap_*`) with hex bolts (`bolt_cap_*`).
  - **Latches & hinges**: 2 multi-part front draw latches (upper catch plates, catch hooks, lower base plates, pivot pins, levers, pull tabs) and 2 rear 3-piece hinges (upper/lower leaves and hinge barrels).
  - **Two side handles**: Recessed backing plates, paired pivot brackets, pivot pins, vertical bail arms, and rubberized grips (`handle_*`).
- **Materials (3 draw calls)**: `mat_olive_body` (olive drab painted steel), `mat_dark_steel` (gunmetal hardware), and `mat_rubber_trim` (matte black rubber). Because the session ran with an image generation limit of `0`, PBR textures were generated procedurally from geometry and material surface descriptions (`kernel.smart_source`) at export time rather than via an image model.

### Verification & Findings
- **Technical checks**: `tier1=ok`, package validation passed, `blender_asset_qa` passed, `USD 0 crit/0 warn`, `godot_4 0 crit/1 warn (godot_4:up_axis_reorient)`, and headless Godot 4 `engine_import` succeeded (`21 s`).
- **Visual QA (unverified preview — judged by uncalibrated generative fallback)**:
  - Overall Tier-1.5 score: **2.60** (below target 3.4 by 0.80)
  - Silhouette: **2.69** (below target 3.3 by 0.61)
  - Shippability: **2.63** (below target 3.4 by 0.77)
  - Because this is an unverified preview (`verified: false`) scored by the uncalibrated fallback, a person should inspect the lookdev render and exported package in Godot 4 before shipping.

pipeline.task:
Make a game-ready 3D prop: a rugged military supply crate kit-bashed from panels, corner guards, latches and two side handles.

Target engine: Godot 4 (import as glTF 2.0 binary).
Blender 5.3 is installed and on PATH as `blender`; run it headless (for example `blender -b --factory-startup --python script.py`). There is no display and no network.

"Game-ready" here means all of the following, checked automatically afterwards:
- Real-world scale in metres (1 unit = 1 m). Up axis: glTF's +Y (Blender's glTF exporter converts Blender's +Z up for you). The prop stands on the ground: its lowest point at height 0, centred on the origin horizontally.
- At most 3000 triangles for the main model.
- Every mesh has a UV map; UV islands inside 0-1 and not overlapping.
- PBR metallic-roughness material(s), at most 3, with image textures: base colour, normal map, and roughness/metallic (an ORM or metallic-roughness texture). Texture sizes are powers of two, at most 2048 px.
- Optional: lower-detail LODs as separate files named <name>_LOD1.glb, <name>_LOD2.glb; a simple collision mesh as a separate object whose name ends in "-col".

Deliver into the folder `output/` of your working directory: exactly one main file `output/<name>.glb` (textures may be embedded) plus the texture images as PNG files in `output/textures/`. When you are done, reply with a short summary of what you made and anything you could not do.

This run is limited to about 45 model calls in total, counting every reply you make; plan so that a complete `output/<name>.glb` exists before then, and prefer delivering a simpler complete asset to an unfinished ambitious one.

unfair: Arm V's screenshots reach the model in two steps: the stock harness puts an MCP tool's image into the conversation only while it is tiny (base64 under about 10 to 16 KB, measured); a larger one, which is every useful render (a 256 px solid view of a cube is 53 KB), is saved to a file and the path returned ('[Resource offloaded to file:///...media_0.png]'), and the agent sees the picture only if it opens that file with view_file (tests/test_compare_agents.py). That is the stock agent's behaviour with any MCP server and is left as it is; each V record counts screenshots taken and opened.

Arm V's Blender has a virtual display (Xvfb) inside the sandbox, because its screenshot is Blender's solid-viewport renderer (Workbench), which needs OpenGL: without a display Blender 5.3 exits at the first render (measured). Arm A's Blender has none, as in round 3; Cycles works without one.

Arm V's Blender binary is mounted in the sandbox (the MCP server starts it) but is not on PATH and not named in its task; an agent that finds it can still run it from the shell. Each record counts shell commands that start Blender (blender_invocations), so a V run that bypassed its MCP server is visible.

Arms V and A run with 0 images: the owner's image allowance is used up (29 of 30), and the relay refuses an image call. A stock agent made no image in round 3 (its textures were procedural); the task text is unchanged.
Arms N and C make their textures as images and are not run until the owner allows more images.

Arm C is told less than the agents: its command line carries the brief, engine and triangle budget, but not the rest of the game-ready list (C_UNEXPRESSED); the pipeline applies its own conventions there.

Arm C's change request is `agy3d edit OUT "<change>"` on a copy of its first output folder: one patch to the shipped design, no image (C_CHANGE_MODE; 'append', a new design from the sentence appended to the prompt, is kept for comparison). The agents' change sessions are new conversations over the files their first session left.

Every arm's task ends with a budget sentence ('about N model calls'), N computed from its share (CALL_MODEL); maxOutputTokens is 16,384 instead of the stock 65,535; web search and URL reading are disabled (no network).

The upstream qa_check / mesh_stats / texel_density scripts are by the author of the skills arm B used (round 1). The Godot import script and the three.js check are this project's own (C's authors); they are applied to the bare GLB of every arm with a manifest holding only the bounds read from that GLB.
The judge is Gemini (gemini-4-carbon, thinking low) judging Gemini-made assets; renders are Blender's (Cycles), not the target engine's.

Rows that only this project can pass are marked so in the scorecard (installed into a project, provenance, the same bytes from the same request): they are reported, not mixed into the shared game-ready rate.
The machine is shared: other test suites may run on its 4 cores during live runs; each record carries the load at its start and end. Wall times are not comparable with an idle machine.
